questions.q: What does the no-cloning theorem actually state?
options: Entangled qubits can never be separated by distance
No unitary operation can take an arbitrary unknown quantum state and produce two independent copies of it
Quantum states can never be measured more than once
Classical bits cannot be copied either
questions.explain: No-cloning is specifically about unknown states and duplication -- there is no fixed procedure that works for every possible |ψ⟩ and produces two independent copies of it.

questions.q: At what point, if any, does teleportation have two independent copies of |ψ⟩ existing at once?
options: Never -- exactly one copy exists on Alice's qubit before the protocol, and exactly one copy exists on Bob's qubit after, with the original destroyed by measurement in between
Briefly, right after Alice's CNOT gate, before her measurement
Permanently, after Bob applies his correction gate
Only if Alice forgets to measure her qubits
questions.explain: Teleportation is destruction-then-recreation, not duplication: Alice's measurement destroys the original superposition on q1 in the same step that makes Bob's corrected q3 usable as |ψ⟩ -- no moment has two copies.

questions.q: Why is superdense coding not even a candidate for violating no-cloning?
options: Because Bob's qubit is destroyed during the protocol, which is explicitly allowed
Because the no-cloning theorem only applies to 3-qubit systems
It never attempts to copy an unknown state at all -- Alice transmits a known, classical 2-bit message using gates she chooses and fully knows
Because superdense coding doesn't use any quantum gates
questions.explain: No-cloning restricts copying of arbitrary unknown states; superdense coding only manipulates a shared Bell pair with gates (I, X, Z, ZX) that Alice selects and knows exactly, so the theorem never applies to it.

questions.q: Why can't Bob extract |ψ⟩ or send information faster than light by measuring his qubit immediately after Alice's measurement, before her classical bits arrive?
options: Because Alice's measurement has no effect on Bob's qubit at all
Because Bob's qubit physically doesn't exist until the classical bits arrive
Averaged over Alice's 4 possible outcomes, Bob's qubit looks like a maximally mixed, informationless state -- he needs the classical bits to know which of the 4 corrections to apply
Because measuring a qubit always destroys all information permanently
questions.explain: Bob's qubit sits in one of 4 different states depending on Alice's outcome, but without knowing which one, it's statistically indistinguishable from a mixed state -- no information is extractable without the classical bits, which travel at or below light speed.

questions.q: A skeptic claims teleportation sends information faster than light because Alice's measurement 'instantly' determines Bob's qubit's state. What is the flaw in this claim?
options: Determining Bob's qubit's state is not the same as Bob being able to read out any usable information from it -- that requires the classical bits, which are not instant
There is no flaw -- the claim is correct and teleportation does send information instantly
Alice's measurement doesn't actually collapse anything
Bob's qubit's state is never actually affected by Alice's measurement
questions.explain: Correlation is not the same as usable, extractable information -- Bob's qubit changing state in a way correlated with Alice's outcome gives Bob nothing readable until the classical message arrives and tells him which correction to apply.
